lead: An array is a group of identical antennas fed from one source so that their fields add in some directions and cancel in others. The smallest array has two elements. Its far-field pattern is the pattern of one element multiplied by an array factor, a term that depends only on the spacing, the wavelength and the phase difference between the two feed currents. Designers use it to point a beam or place a null without redesigning the element, from AM broadcast towers to mobile base-station panels.
prereq: You need: the radiation pattern, the field and power patterns and the half-wave dipole pattern from the antenna fundamentals topic.

sections.h3: The two-source model and the array factor

blocks.text: Take two identical isotropic radiators (an isotropic element radiates equally in every direction). Put element 1 at the origin and element 2 on the +z axis, a distance d away; the z axis is the array axis. Feed element 1 with current I and element 2 with I ejα, so α is the phase by which element 2 leads element 1, in radians. Measure the direction θ from the +z axis.

A far-field point in direction θ is closer to element 2 by the path difference d cosθ. The wave from element 2 therefore arrives ahead in phase by βd cosθ, where β = 2π/λ is the phase constant and λ the free-space wavelength. Adding the feed lead α, the total phase of wave 2 relative to wave 1 is ψ. Adding two equal phasors 1 and e<sup>jψ</sup> and taking the magnitude gives the array factor.

blocks.where: ψ is the total phase difference between the two waves in radians; β = 2π/λ in rad/m; d is the spacing in metres; θ is the angle from the array axis; α is the feed-current phase of element 2 relative to element 1.
AF is the array factor (a field ratio). Its largest value is 2. Dividing by 2 gives the normalized array factor |cos(ψ/2)|, which peaks at 1; the normalized power pattern is cos²(ψ/2).

blocks.text: The waves add fully when ψ = 0, ±2π, … (|AF| = 2) and cancel when ψ = ±π, ±3π, … (AF = 0). Only the values of ψ that a real angle can produce matter: as θ runs from 0° to 180°, cosθ runs from +1 to −1, so ψ sweeps the visible range from βd + α down to −βd + α.

Three cases cover most exam questions. With d = λ/2 and α = 0, ψ = π cosθ: the maximum is at θ = 90° (broadside) and the nulls are at 0° and 180°, along the axis. With d = λ/2 and α = π, the maxima move to both ends of the axis and the null to 90°. With d = λ/4 and α = −π/2, ψ = (π/2)(cosθ − 1): ψ = 0 at θ = 0° and ψ = −π at θ = 180°, so the array fires one way along the axis and is silent the other way. This one-sided cardioid is the idea behind the Yagi-Uda reflector.
A beam points toward the element whose current lags. Measured from broadside instead of from the axis, cosθ becomes sinθ; keep one reference for the whole problem.

Real elements are not isotropic. For identical, identically oriented elements, the total field is the field of one element at the origin times the array factor, because the second element radiates the same shape shifted by d and multiplied by ejψ. This is the principle of pattern multiplication:
E(θ, φ) = E<sub>e</sub>(θ, φ) × AF(θ, φ)
blocks.where: E<sub>e</sub> is the field pattern of one element; AF carries the spacing and phasing; the power pattern is |E<sub>e</sub>|² × |AF|². The nulls of the total pattern are all the nulls of E<sub>e</sub> together with all the nulls of AF.

blocks.text: Two half-wave dipoles mounted parallel to the x axis and spaced along z show it. The dipole has its own null along x, its axis; the array factor adds its nulls along z. The rule also works for groups: an array of identical groups has the pattern of one group times the array factor of the groups. It fails when the elements differ, point different ways, or couple so strongly that their currents are unequal.

examples.question: Two identical isotropic radiators are spaced d = λ/2 along the z axis and element 2 leads element 1 by α = 90°. Find the direction of maximum radiation, the null, and the normalized field and power at θ = 0°, with θ measured from the array axis.
steps: βd = (2π/λ)(λ/2) = π rad and α = π/2 rad, so ψ = π cosθ + π/2.
The visible range of ψ runs from π + π/2 = 3π/2 (at θ = 0°) to −π + π/2 = −π/2 (at θ = 180°).
Maximum: ψ = 0 lies in the range. π cosθ = −π/2 gives cosθ = −0.5, so θ = 120°.
Null: ψ = π lies in the range (ψ = −π does not). π cosθ = π/2 gives cosθ = 0.5, so θ = 60°.
At θ = 0°: ψ = 3π/2 and the normalized field is |cos(3π/4)| = 0.707; the normalized power is 0.707² = 0.5, that is −3 dB.
Half power: |cos(ψ/2)| = 0.707 needs ψ = ±π/2, that is cosθ = 0 or cosθ = −1, so θ = 90° and 180°. The main beam stays above half power from 90° all the way to 180°.
examples.answer: Maximum at θ = 120°, null at θ = 60°; at θ = 0° the field is 0.707 and the power 0.5 (−3 dB) of the maximum. The beam has swung from broadside toward element 1, the lagging element.

examples.question: Four isotropic sources lie on the z axis with spacing λ/2, all fed in phase. Treat them as two pairs: pair A is sources 1 and 2, pair B is sources 3 and 4, and the pair centres are λ apart. Use pattern multiplication to find every null, and check the result at θ = 60°.
steps: One pair (d = λ/2, α = 0) has normalized factor |cos((π/2)cosθ)|, with nulls where (π/2)cosθ = ±π/2, that is θ = 0° and 180°.
The two pair centres are λ apart, in phase: ψ = 2π cosθ and the factor is |cos(π cosθ)|, with nulls where π cosθ = ±π/2, that is cosθ = ±0.5, θ = 60° and 120°.
Total pattern = pair pattern × pair-array factor = |cos((π/2)cosθ)| × |cos(π cosθ)|. Its nulls are the union: θ = 0°, 60°, 120° and 180°.
At θ = 60°: cosθ = 0.5, pair pattern = cos(π/4) = 0.707, group factor = cos(π/2) = 0, product = 0, a null as predicted.
At θ = 75°: pair pattern 0.918 × group factor 0.687 = 0.631, the same as the direct four-element sum.
examples.answer: Nulls at 0°, 60°, 120° and 180° with the main beam at 90°. The same four nulls come out of the N-element formula of the uniform linear array, which confirms the product rule.

traps: Adding the powers of the two elements. Add the fields as phasors, then square: two equal in-phase fields give four times the power of one, not twice.
Getting the sign of βd cosθ backwards. The far point is closer to the element on the +z side, so that element’s wave arrives ahead; with α as its feed lead, ψ = βd cosθ + α.
Setting ψ = 0 for a null. A null needs ψ = ±π, ±3π, …, and only the values inside the visible range βd + α to −βd + α give real angles.
Writing βd = π/2 for d = λ/2. It is π; for d = λ/4 it is π/2. Convert α to radians before adding it.
Forgetting the element’s own nulls. With pattern multiplication the total pattern has every null of the element and every null of the array factor.

quiz.q: Write the array factor of two equal isotropic sources and define ψ.
quiz.a: |AF| = 2|cos(ψ/2)| with ψ = βd cosθ + α; β = 2π/λ, d is the spacing, θ the angle from the array axis and α the feed phase of element 2 relative to element 1.

quiz.q: Why does the d = λ/4, α = −90° pair radiate along +z but not along −z?
quiz.a: Along +z the path lead of element 2 (+90°) cancels its feed lag (−90°), so ψ = 0 and the waves add. Along −z the path term is −90°, so ψ = −180° and the waves cancel.

quiz.q: Two in-phase isotropic sources are spaced λ/2 apart. Find the maximum and the nulls.
quiz.a: ψ = π cosθ. Maximum at ψ = 0: θ = 90°. Nulls at ψ = ±π: cosθ = ±1, so θ = 0° and 180°.

quiz.q: For the d = λ/4, α = −90° pair, find the normalized field at θ = 90° and θ = 120°.
With d = λ/2, how does the beam move as α rises from 0 to π?
quiz.a: The maximum satisfies cosθ = −α/π, so it moves from 90° (α = 0) toward 180°. At α = π a second equal maximum appears at θ = 0°, so the array fires at both ends of the axis.

quiz.q: Two half-wave dipoles parallel to x are spaced λ/2 along z and fed in phase. Find the directions of zero radiation in the x-z plane.
quiz.a: The element has a null along its own axis, ±x (θ = 90° and 270°). The array factor |cos((π/2)cosθ)| has nulls along ±z (θ = 0° and 180°). The total pattern is zero in all four directions and has four lobes between them.

beyond: Not for the exam. Pattern multiplication is the starting point of every beamformer: a base-station panel or a car radar multiplies a fixed element pattern by an array factor that software sets. Real arrays depart from the product rule because neighbouring elements couple, so engineers measure or simulate an “embedded element pattern” for each position and use that instead. Search for embedded element pattern, mutual coupling in arrays and directional AM arrays.

figure.caption: The field pattern of the first worked example in a plane through the array axis. With element 2 leading by 90°, the beam swings to 120°, back toward the lagging element 1, and the null sits at 60°; along the axis at 0° the field is 0.707 of the peak.

spec.aria: Polar plot of a two-element array pattern: elements 1 and 2 on a horizontal axis, a lobe pointing up-left at 120 degrees, a null at 60 degrees, and the field 0.707 along the axis to the right.
